title: Predicting Replication Rates with Z-Curve: A Brief Exploratory Validation Study Using the Replication Database

selection.evidence: Reached 2026-11-05 from the FReD data paper (it lists this preprint as one of two existing uses of the database). Ships code + data (osf k4d6w). Prior suspicion stated before running: the stratified-on-outcome sampling design forces variance in the replication rate, so a high r may be manufactured by the design. (The opened-log line was written after K1/K2 had run; the suspicion itself was written in-session before z01 was launched.)

cost.compute_notes: Preprint PDF (16 pp, all read). OSF k4d6w: R script, red data CSV (1,072 usable rows), results CSVs, figures -- 13 files, checksums verified. Docker image zoo-r-zcurve:4.4.1 (zoo-r-psych:4.4.1 + CRAN zcurve, openxlsx). z01: reproduction + K1-K4, 1,000 samples each (~45 min wall-clock); z02: fixed-n and multilevel controls, 600 samples each; z03: permutation null of r.

triggers: validating a replicability estimator with a replication database
expected replication rate ERR vs actual replication rate
stratified sampling on the outcome inflates correlation
estimator correlates with truth across constructed samples

claims.statement: Across 10,000 samples drawn from FReD with target replication rates uniform on (0,1), z-curve's ERR correlates with the actual replication rate r = .945 (abstract: .933) and EDR r = .881; ERR is compressed toward the mean (SD .13 vs .25) and a linear recalibration RR = 1.850 ERR - .573 (R2 .893) predicts RR within about +-16%.
claims.scope: 1,072 entries from the 2023-10-02 FReD version; each sample = 30%·P of successes + 30%·(1-P) of failures; z = |r| / sqrt((1-r^2)/(n-2)); RR = mean of significant_replication.

quantities.name: zcurve_err_rr_correlation_stratified_design
quantities.baseline: paper .945 (10,000 samples); slope 1.79 (1.85), intercept -.547 (-.573), M RR .431, M ERR .546

quantities.name: zcurve_sample_size_per_draw_median
quantities.baseline: paper text says 'samples from 322 studies'; the code's sampler gives 127-195

our_assessment.why: Reproduces, and does not mean what it is taken to mean. With the originals' z PERMUTED across rows (no z-outcome link at all) the same design returns r = .645; with z-curve replaced by the share of z > 2.8 it returns .945, identical to z-curve; at fixed n a single random permutation already gives r = -.30. Samples are mixtures of two fixed pools in proportion P, so any statistic whose pool means differ tracks P with little noise. The r is a property of the design, not evidence of the estimator's validity.

claims.statement: z-curve is 'a valid and economic method to compare replicability estimates for large sets of studies'; a linear transformation of ERR 'could lead to a precise and valid estimator of replication rate'.
claims.scope: Conclusion section; the author notes the analysis is exploratory and the linear model was not tested on new data.

quantities.name: zcurve_err_minus_rr_natural_subsamples
quantities.baseline: natural random 30% subsamples: M ERR .520 vs M RR .393; r(ERR, RR) .369 with SD RR only .025

quantities.name: zcurve_mean_abs_err_minus_rr_across_source_projects
quantities.baseline: CORE .66/.76, ML1 .59/.50, ML3 .08/.44, OSC 2015 .33/.64, RRR1 .24/.57, individual submissions .14/.57 (RR/ERR); Pearson .579, Spearman .600, mean signed ERR - RR +.242 (z02 K4)

quantities.name: zcurve_err_rr_r_one_row_per_original_fixed_n60
quantities.baseline: paper design with one random row per original (multilevel structure removed), fixed n = 60

our_assessment.why: The test that would support comparing literatures is ERR vs RR across REAL literatures. Across the six source projects in the same deposit ERR ranks them roughly (Spearman .60, Pearson .58, n = 6) but misses by .27 on average (signed +.24) and overestimates five of six. The recalibration slope is fitted to an artificial two-pool mixture; its value is set by the pools, so it has no reason to transfer.

claims.statement: At the row level, the originals' z in this deposit does discriminate replicated from failed findings: AUC .737 for significant_replication (.720 for the success code), higher than the .625 found in the 2026 FReD export with z computed from reported p (roseler2024 #c3); part of the gap is that z = r/se here grows with n.
claims.scope: 1,004 rows with computable z; not clustered by original.

our_assessment.why: Computed directly. This is the honest content of the paper's result: a row-level association, which the design converts into r near 1.

datasheet.composition: FReD export: one row per original-replication effect pair (70 columns).
datasheet.caveats: Per-lab Many Labs rows; the analysis ignores the multilevel structure (the author says so). Blinding: aggregates only were printed (mark's control).

relations.why: Both validate a replication predictor; on the same database the row-level discrimination is modest (AUC .58-.74) whatever the aggregate correlation says.
